newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan bank closures seen key to financial cleanup.
newsitem.headline: Japan bank closures seen key to financial cleanup.

text.p: A move by Japanese authorities to liquidate a troubled regional bank on Thursday was greeted not with shock and horror but rather relief that more steps were being taken to clean up the nation's bad loan mess.

The Finance Ministry said it had suspended most business of Hanwa Bank Ltd, a second-tier regional bank based in western Japan, because the bank could not recover its bad loans and was unable to operate as a going concern.
Authorities said, however, that depositors would be protected and stressed that swift handling of failed banks was in fact vital for the recovery of Japan's financial system.

"The Bank of Japan believes that prompt measures to deal with insolvent financial institutions without delay will lead to the early rejuvenation of the Japanese financial system," Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita said in a statement.
Financial analysts agreed that the decision to wind up Hanwa -- without waiting for a run on the bank by depositors -- was a welcome sign after years of regulatory reluctance to act.
"I wouldn't characterise this as a banking problem, I would characterise this as the beginning of a cleanup," said James McGuinness, an analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson International.
"This is what everyone has been wanting -- for them to take a proactive stance," he added.

Japan saw its first postwar banking failure last year after a run by depositors on Hyogo Bank, a regional bank also based in western Japan. Hyogo's business was transferred to a new bank. Another small regional bank failed earlier this year, but like Hyogo was replaced by a new bank.
Hanwa, however, will be wound up, although a "new bank" will be created to handle the liquidation process.
Much of Japan's financial system has been hit hard by the collapse of real estate prices from the sky-high levels of the 1980s "bubble" era, when property and share prices soared.
Big banks have written off large chunks of their bad loans but smaller institutions still face problems.
"There can't be a cleanup of the system without further failures," McGuinness said.

Analysts said, however, that the Hanwa case highlighted the need for Japan's financial institutions to improve disclosure of business data, especially as Tokyo moves to free its markets of the restraints of government regulations and interference.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto last week unveiled a five-year "Big Bang" plan to liberalise Tokyo financial markets by 2001 and catch up with reforms in Europe and North America.
Hanwa on November 5 announced it had revised its forecast for parent current earnings for the six months to September to a loss of 280 million yen ($2.52 million).

On Thursday, the bank said it posted a six-month parent current loss of 33.72 billion yen ($303 million). The Finance Ministry said it had problem loans of 190 billion yen ($1.71 billion), but its capital was only 20.3 billion yen ($182 million) at the end of September.

Japanese media reports said Hanwa's auditors had been reluctant to approve the bank's earnings statement for the six months to September, which was set for release on Friday. The auditors were not available for comment.

"Actually, that's terribly positive if the auditors did their jobs and protected the interests of shareholders rather than the interests of management," said David Threadgold, a financial analyst at BZW Securities. "Auditors have always been a carpet over which management walked."
Analysts also said better banking supervision by authorities would be vital as Japan deregulated its markets.

"It certainly behoves financial authorities...to ensure that there is greater perspicacity in bank reporting and greater oversight by the authorities who police these institutions in a deregulated environment," said Brian Waterhouse, a financial analyst at James Capel Pacific.

Politicians are now debating whether to create a financial oversight body separate from the Finance Ministry, which in recent years has faced criticism for its handling of the nation's bad loan woes. ($1=111 yen)
